title: Atom — Bohr's model and hydrogen spectrum
topicTitle: Atom — Bohr's model and hydrogen spectrum
notes: Bohr's hydrogen atom keeps a positive nucleus and an electron in orbit, and adds the rule that the angular momentum is n h / (2π). Only integer n is allowed.
In an allowed orbit the electron does not radiate, even though it is accelerating. Radiation happens only when the electron jumps from one allowed energy to a lower one.
The energies are E_n = −13.6 / n^2 electronvolts. The ground state is n = 1, at −13.6 eV. The zero of energy is the electron removed to infinity.
The photon energy is the difference of the two levels. A jump from n = 3 to n = 2 is a Balmer line. Jumps that end on n = 1 are the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet.
The wave formula is 1/λ = R (1/n1^2 − 1/n2^2). R is the Rydberg constant. A larger jump gives a larger photon energy and a shorter wavelength.
The model gives the hydrogen numbers and fails for atoms with several electrons. It also does not explain why the angular momentum should be quantised. Later wave mechanics supplies that reason.

universalFacts: Bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy En = −13.6 eV·Z²/n² (for H, Z=1).
Rydberg/Balmer series: 1/λ = R(H)(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Absorption/emission = ΔE = hν between levels.
Four quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0…n−1), mₗ (orientation, −l…+l), mₛ (spin ±½). Orbitals: s (spherical), p (dumbbell).
